_comment: Language-neutral parity fixtures: each runs in BOTH the JS engine and ancir_runtime.py; outputs/results are compared within tolerance. The JS emitter is the single source of input DATA: 'generate' specs (seeded rhythm/groups/linear) are realised in JS and written into js_results.json so Python analyses identical arrays. Column refs in args use '@ref' tokens. tableProcess outputs compare by CANONICAL key (trailing _<id> stripped: cosinory_13 -> cosinory). tableProcessResult compares named fields of the single comparison. Add a fixture = add an entry. See tools/README-parity.md.

fixtures._comment: FIT-8. Every third hourly epoch missing: IV divides the squared successive differences by the valid successive pairs (Witting et al. 1990), not by n - 1. The old divisor reported about a third of the IV here.

fixtures.note: NPCRA on a NUMBER x (hourly from 0) with the FIRST and LAST times missing. computeNPCRA kept every row whose Number(t) is finite, and Number(null) is 0, so both rows became samples at hour 0: the epoch grid started an hour early and their y values were averaged into the first epoch. A missing time is now dropped (isInvalidValue), which the Python and R ports already did.
Three groups with the post-hoc test switched OFF: the ANOVA itself is unchanged and postHoc is an empty list (a port that ignored the switch would return the Tukey-Kramer rows).

A correlogram of a BinnedData output on a TIME input: 1 h bins stepping 0.5 h (diffStep), so the x column's binWidth (1) is twice its spacing. The app takes the lag step from the column's binWidth; the Python export estimated it from the spacing (0.5).
An imported 'bin' column (binWidth 0.75 h on a 0.5 h step, as the Enspire wells schema creates). The app's lag step is the binWidth, 0.75; the Python export used the spacing, 0.5.

A plain NUMBER x starting at 5 h whose spacing cycles 1, 1, 1.05 h (within 10% of the median, so the index-shift path). The app's lag step was the MEAN spacing, (last - first) / (n - 1) = 1.0167 h, until SPEC-10 moved it to the median, 1 h, over hoursSinceStart (the offset itself changes nothing: the autocorrelation is shift-invariant). Since the lag window is set by time (correlogram.js rule 5), it ends at half the span, 238.9 / 2 h, so 119 steps: one more than n / 2 = 118 of the 236 rows, which capped it before.

Two series. The first is a TIME x whose spacing alternates 0.25 and 0.75 h (not uniform, so the time-pair path), with maxLag 30 h and minLag 2 h saved on the SERIES as the app saves them; the lag step is the upper median spacing, 0.25 h (96 spacings of 0.25 h against 95 of 0.75 h; SPEC-10, it was the mean spacing, 0.5 h, before), so the half-hour slots (k + 0.5 h) hold no pairs and are reported as missing (null; they read r = 0 before the empty-slot fix), and the Python export once read plot-level corrMaxLag / corrMinLag keys the app never writes. The second is a regular hourly time series on the auto lag range. The first series' saved maxLag of 30 h was capped at n / 2 steps, 96 x 0.25 = 24 h, before the lag window was set by time (correlogram.js rule 5); the user's 30 h now wins, so its rows run from 2 to 30 h.

Two series whose x has a missing END, no binWidth, so the lag step is the median interval of the valid times (SPEC-10; it was the mean spacing when this fixture was written). The first is a NUMBER x from 5 h, hourly, with the LAST time missing; the second a TIME x every 0.5 h with the FIRST time missing. The app used (t[n-1] - t[0]) / (n-1) over the raw rows and read the missing end as 0: the first series got a step of about -5/(n-1), negative, so the plot was blank, and the second a step of 0.5 * (n-2)/(n-1), so every lag was mislabelled. The step became (t_j - t_i) / (j - i) over the first and last VALID rows; since SPEC-10 it is the median interval, which skips missing rows by construction.

SPEC-10. A NUMBER x, hourly for 7 days, with the rows from 50 h to 62 h REMOVED (a recording gap with no rows), no binWidth. The plot's lag step was the mean spacing, (last - first) / (n - 1) = 167 / 155 = 1.077 h, so every lag slot sat off the hour and the dominant period read wrong; it is now the median interval, 1 h, as the Rhythmicity node's correlogram uses (computeAutocorrelation with binSize null). Since the lag window is set by time (correlogram.js rule 5), it ends at half the span, 167 / 2 h, so 83 h; n / 2 of the 156 rows stopped it at 78 h.

computeAutocorrelation with no binSize (how RhythmicityAnalysis and MovingAnalysis call it) on spacings 1,1,1,2,2,2: the app's step is the UPPER median, the element at floor(len / 2) of the sorted spacings (2), not the mean of the middle two (1.5, what np.median and R's median give), so the lags are 2 and 4 h, not 1.5, 3 and 4.5 h. Its lag slots were also the old overlapping ones: three pairs exactly 1 h apart (half the 2 h step) were counted at lag 0 AND at lag 2, and two pairs 3 h apart at lag 2 AND lag 4, and lag 0 left out each sample's pairing with itself, so it read -0.142 instead of 1. With lag 0 defined as 1 and half-open slots [(k - 1/2) dt, (k + 1/2) dt) (utils/correlogram.js), the correlations are 1, 0.0423, -0.0941 (were -0.142, -0.140, -0.331).

Pairs exactly on a lag-slot boundary. Uneven times (the time-pair path) with the step given as 1 h and minLag 1 h (so lag 0 is out of it): many separations are exactly 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 ... h, half-way between two lags. Slots are half-open, lag k takes (k - 1/2) dt <= d < (k + 1/2) dt, so each such pair is counted once, in the UPPER lag. The old window |d - k dt| <= dt / 2 counted it in both.

Distinct samples closer than half a step. Uneven times with four near-coincident pairs (0.1, 0.2, 0.05 and 0.3 h apart) and a 1 h step. Lag 0 is exactly 1 by definition; the near-zero pairs estimate the correlation at a small NON-zero lag, so they are not used at any lag (they are below the lag-1 slot). The old code excluded each sample's pairing with itself and averaged only the near-zero pairs, so lag 0 was their correlation, not 1.

Lag slots that hold no pair. Six days of a 24 h rhythm (plus Gaussian noise, sd 4, written out here) sampled at alternating 0.25 and 0.75 h spacing, starting and ending on a 0.25 h step, so the median step is 0.25 h and every separation is a whole hour plus 0, 0.25 or 0.75 h: each k + 0.5 h slot is empty. An empty slot is missing (NaN, written null), not r = 0 (utils/correlogram.js rule 4). With r = 0 the first empty slot in the trough read as the return to non-negative and the peak search answered a mid-trough lag; util-autocorrelation-peak-empty-slots compares that peak. Since the lag window is set by time (correlogram.js rule 5), it ends at half the span, 72 h (289 lags); n / 2 of the 290 samples stopped it at 145 steps, 36.25 h.

Two series starting on different days, the second with a leading gap and a coarser step. The app folds BOTH at the earliest valid sample over all series, snapped to that day's midnight (4 March), so series 1's first bar lands in period 2, not period 1 of its own day.

Display zone America/New_York: the first sample (03:40Z on 8 March) is 22:40 on 7 March there, so rows start at New York midnight on 7 March (05:00Z), not UTC midnight on 8 March. The record crosses the 10 March DST change, which must not move the rows.
One series in UTC whose first sample is 06:20, not midnight, on a 0.3 h step that never lands on a row boundary, so every row's first and last bar is split at the boundary.
A number x axis starting at 5 h with 23.5 h rows: bars sit at the raw x (no start-of-day snap), split at multiples of 23.5.

A BinnedData node's output on a TIME input starting at midnight: the output is a time column of bin STARTS (epoch ms) carrying binWidth = binSize and originTime_ms = the input's first sample. binSize 1.5 h, so rows split bars at 0, 1.5, 3, ... and a bar straddles no boundary; the day boundary 24 h is a multiple.
The same on an input whose first sample (the output's originTime_ms) is 06:20Z, in the America/New_York display zone: bars start at 06:20Z = 01:20 New York, 1.333 h into row 1, and are 1 h wide.

A BinnedData node's output on a NUMBER input starting at 5 h: a 'bin' column whose raw values are bin starts (5, 6, 7, ...) and whose getData is the centres. The actogram places bars at the raw starts, not the centres.

An imported 'bin' column (as the Enspire multiplate wells schema creates) carrying binWidth 0.75 h on a 0.5 h step (so the bars are the column's binWidth wide, not the scanned step) and originTime_ms at 07:30Z, plotted with a time series whose first sample is 02:00Z. Its bars shift by the origin's time of day: raw start 0 lands at 7.5 h in row 1.

fixtures._comment: FIT-12. Half-hourly samples (two per 1 h bin per day) over 7 days with every fifth value missing, so days contribute unequal counts to a bin. Each day's samples in a bin are averaged first; the profile is the mean of the day means and the SEM is across days (n = days), not across the pooled samples (pseudo-replication; Hurlbert 1984).

fixtures.note: FIT-11: timed (amplitude-weighted) mode reports R and the weighted acrophase only; z and pvalue are NaN, because the weighted Rayleigh p changes when a constant baseline is added to the series.
The tp-watsonwilliams-2groups angles with the Watson-Williams test switched OFF (showWatsonWilliams false): the per-column Rayleigh results are reported and F / ww_pvalue are not computed.

Pins the cross-language cleaning rule for blank cells: '' and whitespace-only strings are MISSING data (skipped), never coerced to 0; the genuine 0 and the numeric string '3' are data. Python's float('') raises and R's as.numeric(' ') is NA, so both always treated blanks as absent - isNaN('')===false made JS the outlier until isInvalidValue closed the hole. Valid values are [5, 0, 7, 3, 2]: n=5, mean=3.4.

fixtures.rToleranceWhy: R's shapiro.test and the JS port both implement Royston AS R94 and agree on W to 2.8e-11; only the p-value's normalising transform differs, by 5.4e-8. That is a tail-approximation coefficient difference, not a disagreement about the statistic, so R is held to 1e-6 here while Python stays at the default.

fixtures.note: Pins utils/qq.js qqPoints (Blom positions + Acklam quantile + quartile line + pointwise envelope) against scipy. scipy.stats.probplot defaults to Filliben positions, NOT Blom, so the Python side computes the positions explicitly — norm.ppf((arange(1,n+1)-0.375)/(n+0.25)) — matching the JS (and the Shapiro-Wilk m-value convention). Quartiles use np.quantile's default linear (type-7) interpolation, matching describeStats and utils/qq.js. The R side is a genuine third opinion: qnorm/dnorm rather than Acklam or ndtri, with the same explicit Blom positions (R's own ppoints() drops the 3/8 constant above n = 10) and quantile(type = 7). rTolerance 1e-6 (same order as the other Acklam-vs-exact fixtures, e.g. util-normality-shapiro): JS's normalQuantile is only accurate to ~1.15e-9, and dividing by dnorm(z) in the band SE amplifies that to ~1e-8 absolute in bandLo/bandHi — R's exact qnorm and scipy's exact ndtri agree with EACH OTHER far tighter than either does with JS's approximation, which is the expected shape of this disagreement, not a bug.

Pins the probability-plot correlation r the Q-Q plot displays (utils/qq.js qqCorrelation, also its qq_r metric column) against scipy.stats.pearsonr of the sorted sample vs norm.ppf at the same BLOM positions the plot draws. Filliben's original statistic uses Filliben positions; Blom is deliberate, matching the drawn quantiles (see util-qq-points-normal). Same 16-value input (one null) as that fixture, so n also pins the clean-count.

fixtures._comment: Peak-of-the-correlogram convention, checked in all three languages. X is a triangle wave of period 8 correlated with ITSELF, so r is exactly +1 at lag 0 and exactly -1 at lags -4 and +4. A sign-blind argmax that keeps the first winner reports lag -4 with r = -1; the peak must be lag 0 with r = +1.

The peak of an AUTOcorrelogram is the dominant PERIOD, which is a different question from the cross-correlogram's peak and needs a different rule. The input is a triangle wave of period 6 sampled 40 times. Lag 0 is exactly 1 by definition, so an argmax over every lag answers 0 and says nothing (what the Python and R ports did). The repeats at 12 and 18 are normalised by ever fewer overlapping pairs and come out ABOVE the one at 6, so an argmax that merely skips lag 0 answers 18 (what the JS did). The peak is the largest correlation in the first positive lobe: lag 6.

fixtures.note: The dominant-period peak on the plot-correlogram-empty-slots data (every k + 0.5 h lag slot empty). With empty slots read as r = 0, the first one in the trough counted as the return to non-negative, so the peak was a mid-trough lag with r = 0. Read as missing, the peak is near 24 h.

The lag window is set by TIME, not by the sample count (utils/correlogram.js rule 5). Three days of a 24 h rhythm with a 12 h harmonic (50 + 20 cos(2 pi t / 24) + 6 cos(4 pi (t - 3) / 24), no noise, written out here) at alternating 0.25 and 0.75 h spacing: 146 samples over 72.25 h, median step 0.25 h. The old cap of n / 2 steps (73 x 0.25 h) stopped the correlogram at 18.25 h, before the 24 h peak could appear; the default window is now half the span, 36.125 h, so 145 lags from 0 to 36 h. No noise, because the slots either side of 24 h (23.75 and 24.25 h) read within 0.002 of it on a clean rhythm, so noise would decide which of the three is the peak; this fixture pins the window. util-autocorrelation-peak-uneven-3day compares the peak (24 h).

The dominant-period peak on the plot-correlogram-uneven-3day data. With the window capped at n / 2 steps (18.25 h) there was no 24 h lag to find, and the peak read the last lag on the rising flank, 18.25 h at r = 0.04; with the window at half the span (36 h) the peak is 24 h.
FDRCorrection method 'none': the p-values pass through unadjusted and reject is p <= alpha.
FDRCorrection Bonferroni: p times the number of non-missing tests, capped at 1.

A NUMBER x (hourly from 0) whose LAST time is missing. The node coerced its times with Number, so the missing row went into the FFT at t = 0: the FFT's own step came out negative, it returned an empty spectrum and the observed statistic was 0. The same coercion made the hours-to-samples step for the block bootstrap (t[n-1] - t[0]) / (n-1) read the end as 0. The node now keeps the rows where x and y are both present (as both ports always did) and takes the step from the first and last present times (utils/validPairs.js meanSpacing, shared with the Correlogram). Only `observed` is compared: the p-value is Monte Carlo (see Known boundaries).

A TIME x (every hour from 2024-03-04T00:00Z) whose FIRST timestamp is missing. hoursSinceStart keeps it as null and starts the rest at 0, so the old Number coercion put the missing row at t = 0 beside the real first sample and its y went into the FFT. The observed statistic is now computed on the present (x, y) rows only, as in both ports.
oddsRatio is Infinity here; JSON cannot represent it, so only the p-value is compared. The Infinity case is covered by the JS unit test.

fixtures.rToleranceWhy: Same cause as util-normality-shapiro: R's shapiro.test and the JS port both implement Royston AS R94 and agree on W, but the p-value's normalising transform differs in the 8th significant figure. Surfaces here because the analysis reports the p-value. Python stays at the default tolerance.

fixtures.note: n = 5000, the top of Royston's validated range: W and its p-value in all three. Crosses with tp-normalitytest-shapiro-n5001.
fixtures.rToleranceWhy: As tp-normalitytest-shapiro: R's shapiro.test p-value transform differs from the JS in the 8th significant figure; W agrees.

fixtures.note: n = 5001: W in all three (R computes it from the Royston weights, since shapiro.test refuses n > 5000), the p-value and the verdict missing in all three.
fixtures.rToleranceWhy: As tp-normalitytest-shapiro: R's shapiro.test p-value transform differs from the JS in the 8th significant figure; W agrees.

fixtures.note: D'Agostino-Pearson K2 omnibus (skewness and kurtosis z-scores combined, chi-squared on 2 df) on 80 normal readings: the method no fixture reached.

Jarque-Bera on a week of hourly readings (168) of a 24 h rhythm (amplitude 20, noise sd 3): a cosine sampled evenly is bimodal and platykurtic (kurtosis about 1.5 against 3), so this is a realistic NON-normal case and the test rejects (normal = 0).
Spearman rank correlation of a noisy linear pair (n 60), with its p-value and CI: the method no fixture reached.
Cross-correlation with Spearman's rank correlation at each lag (n 80, max lag 5): the method no fixture reached.

fixtures.rToleranceWhy: R fits with glm(family = binomial), an independent IRLS from the JS and statsmodels ones. Coefficients and odds ratios agree exactly; the standard errors, built from the final iteration's weights, differ by ~5e-9 once glm's epsilon is tightened to 1e-12 (at its 1e-8 default the gap is ~5e-5). That is the convergence limit of two separate implementations, not a formula disagreement. Python stays at the default tolerance.

fixtures.note: STAT-24: a 0/1 outcome with missing cells (null, 'NaN', whitespace) is still binary; those rows are dropped instead of the outcome being refused as a third level.
fixtures.rToleranceWhy: As tp-logisticregression: R's glm IRLS and the JS IRLS agree on coefficients; standard errors differ at the ~1e-8 convergence limit.

fixtures.note: Simulate Data with a short-day active fraction: alphaFraction 0.3 on a 24 h square wave sampled every 0.5 h for 3 days, so each cycle is active while t mod 24 < 7.2 (samples 0 to 7.0 h; until v81.11 the time was floored first, so the active phase ran to 7.5 h, t in [0, 8) h). A second section keeps the 0.5 default (key absent) at a 25 h period: active while t mod 25 < 12.5 (samples 0 to 12.0 h; it ran to 12.5 h, t in [0, 13) h, before). Noise is off: the Python port draws noise from numpy rather than the app's seeded minstd stream (exports bake this node's data), so only the noise-free rhythm can be compared. Time is not compared (JS writes ISO strings, Python epoch ms). There is no R port of this node (R exports bake it).

A negative phase shift (the UI allows down to -50 h) with a long-day alphaFraction of 0.75. JS's % keeps the dividend's sign, so the early samples (t + phase < 0) all read as active; Python's % follows the divisor's sign and folded them into the cycle instead, until the port switched to math.fmod.

The exact active/rest boundary at the default active fraction (0.5, key absent) on periods whose half is not a whole hour, sampled every 0.25 h. 25 h: active while t mod 25 < 12.5, so 12.25 h is active and 12.5 h is rest (12.5 h each way; the old floor made it 13 h active, 12 h rest). 23.5 h with a 2.3 h phase shift: active while (t + 2.3) mod 23.5 < 11.75. The 24 h default (boundary 12 h, a whole hour) is unchanged sample for sample. Noise is off (see tp-simulateddata-alpha-fraction).

fixtures.rToleranceWhy: Nonlinear fit: R reaches the optimum with optim(L-BFGS-B) + an analytic Jacobian, scipy with trust-region least_squares. They agree to ~1e-8 on the fitted parameters, which is inside 1e-6 but not the 1e-9 default.

fixtures._comment: A y that is mostly blank leaves 4 rows with both x and y: fewer than the 5 a one-curve free-period cosinor (4 parameters) needs. Every language declines the fit (no outputs) rather than put 4 parameters through 4 points; the JS node also says why (Cosinor.nulls.test.js).
Free period inside an explicit range (20 to 28 h). Pins the bounded optimiser, the periodogram-seeded start and the acrophase (time of peak) convention for free fits in all three languages.
fixtures.rToleranceWhy: Nonlinear fit: R uses optim(L-BFGS-B), scipy trust-region least_squares, JS Levenberg-Marquardt; all reach the same bounded optimum to ~1e-8.

fixtures._comment: A weak 24 h rhythm on a strong linear trend with the default 1 to 48 h range. Unbounded, the free fit followed the trend out of the circadian range; now every language stops on the 48 h bound (and the JS node warns).

FIT-7. A weak 24 h rhythm (amplitude 0.4) in noise (SD 2): the zero-amplitude test is not significant (pvalue >= 0.05), so the acrophase CI is undetermined (NaN) in all three ports, while the point estimate is still reported (Bingham et al. 1982; Cornelissen 2014).

FIT-7, the per-harmonic test. A strong 12 h rhythm plus a weak 24 h one (amplitude 0.45, noise SD 1.5), fitted at 24 h with two harmonics: the model is significant (pvalue < 0.05) through H2, and H1's interval is narrower than a period, but H1's own (beta, gamma) Wald F-test is not significant, so the H1 acrophase CI ports are NaN. Without the per-harmonic test they were finite.
Short (1.4 cycle) fixed-period record, where cov(beta, gamma) is not negligible: pins the delta-method amplitude CI (full covariance) and the time-of-peak acrophase CI, JS vs Python.

fixtures.note: BinnedData on a TIME input (first sample 06:20Z). The app's x output is a time column of bin STARTS in epoch ms (origin + start hours), which getData returns unchanged. The ports used to write bin-centre HOURS into a time column, read back as milliseconds.

The app's saved arg names: aggFunction (not aggFunc) picks the aggregate, and stepSize (default 0.25) is only used when diffStep is true, otherwise the step is binSize. Here aggFunction 'max', binSize 2, stepSize 0.25, diffStep false: 2 h bins on a 2 h step, max of each.

diffStep TRUE: overlapping 3 h windows stepping by stepSize 1 h, median of each. The app's headless compute (definition.func, used by this emitter, the MCP engine and the demo generator) used to ignore diffStep and step by binSize, so it disagreed with the node's own panel; both now read the step from args through one rule.

The app's binData used to filter pairs with the global isFinite, and isFinite(null) is true, so a null y was averaged in as 0 (and became the bin min, reported as null) and a null x put its y in the bin at 0; the Python and R ports already dropped them. clz32 counts leading zero bits of ToUint32(x): truncate, then wrap mod 2^32 (so -1 -> 0xFFFFFFFF -> 0, 2^32 -> 0 -> 32, clz32(0) = 32, 1e20 wraps exactly).

fround rounds to the nearest float32, ties to even: subnormals (1e-40), below half the smallest subnormal to 0 (1e-46), exactly half the smallest subnormal ties to 0, just under halfway past the largest float32 rounds down, exactly halfway overflows to Infinity (missing), 16777217 -> 16777216 (tie to even).

atan2 takes (y, x) in that order, like JS, Python math.atan2 and R atan2; quadrants and the signed-zero rules: atan2(0, -0) = pi and atan2(-0, -1) = -pi (the -0 comes from unary minus).

hypot is variadic (1, 2, 3 and 4 arguments here); a missing argument (null, blank) makes the row missing even though JS Math.hypot(NaN, Infinity) would be Infinity; no overflow for 1e200 (scaled), but 1e308 x 4 overflows (missing).

imul multiplies the ToInt32 forms and wraps to a signed 32-bit result: imul(2^31 - 1, 2) = -2, imul(65537, 65537) = 131073, imul(4294967295, 5) = -5, imul(3.9, 2.9) = 6 (truncates), imul(-2^31, -1) = -2^31, and 1e20 and 2^53 wrap exactly. R needs 16-bit halves: the full product of two int32 is not exact in a double. The last three products are past 2^53 with odd factors, so a plain double product would lose the low bits.
